notes.decision: Translated 'mortifies' (the body). Unattested form; tentatively from ⲱⲗⲉ 'afflict, distress' with Lyc. prosthetic ⲟ-vowel and ⲁ-shift. The Manichaean ascetic context (the holy man bringing the body under the discipline of fasting in order to grasp/restrain the archontic) supports a verb of bodily affliction/subjugation. Alternative readings 'releases/loosens' (from ⲟⲩⲱⲗ 'depart') or 'purifies' are possible but less precise. Flagged for parallel attestation.

Subject of the chain of feminine 3sg verbs (ϣⲁⲥ-ⲧⲟⲩⲃⲟ, ⲛ̄ⲥ-ⲕⲁⲑⲁⲣⲓϩⲉ, ⲛ̄ⲥ-ⲥⲱⲧϥ̄, ⲛ̄ⲥ-ⲉⲓⲱⲉ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ) is taken as the fast (ⲧⲛⲏⲥⲧⲓⲁ, fem.) — the topic of the kephalaion. The four verbs purify/cleanse/filter/wash-out the soul that enters through the nourishment, removing the mingling of darkness from her. This reading aligns with the chapter's structuring of the fast as agent of purification.
Read as scribal abbreviation for ⲣ̄ ('do/become'). The full reading ϣⲁⲣⲉ ⲡⲓⲣⲱⲙⲉ ⲉⲧⲙⲙⲉⲩ ⲣ̄ ⲟⲩⲡⲉⲧⲟⲩⲁⲃⲉ = 'this man habitually becomes a holy one.'

'they are not injured by it.' ϣⲱⲟⲉ tentatively from ϣⲱⲱϥ 'be defiled, harmed' or ϣⲱⲟⲩ 'be dry/wasted.' The phrase ⲛ̄ⲥⲉϣⲱⲟⲉ ⲁⲣⲁⲥ with negative ⲉⲛ implied or following = the sons of light suffer no harm from the nourishment. Tentative; flagged for parallels.

Idiomatic 'they hold their hands back from hand' = they restrain their hands from striking against any other hand. The Manichaean elect refused to inflict harm on any creature because of the Living Soul mingled in matter; restraining the hand is an emblem of nonviolence in defense of the Cross of Light upon which the Soul is suspended.

'when they perform.' ⲟⲱ tentatively from ⲟⲩⲱ 'complete, finish' (already-done auxiliary) used here as full lexical verb 'perform/fulfill.' The conjunctive context ⲉⲧⲉ ⲡⲉ ⲡⲉⲓ̈ 'that is, this is' confirms the verb expresses the act of fulfilling the four works. Tentative.

Preserved as 'ⲟⲑ' since the symbol functions as a chapter-divider ornament rather than a translatable word. Manichaean codices use such marks to bracket chapter titles; here it appears alone on line 9 and twice flanking the heading on line 10.

Preserved untranslated as decorative section/title-frame marker. The pattern 'leer ⲧ̄ⲧ ... ⲧ̄ⲧ' frames the chapter heading on lines 3-5, paralleling the page-header decoration '> · ⲛⲕⲉⲫⲁⲗⲁⲓⲟⲛ · <'.
